picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Activewear is their top category_affinity and they buy performance apparel 4+ workouts a week, with low-medium price sensitivity against an ~$85 AOV that matches their $88 typical spend.
lean_into: technical fabrics — recycled ocean plastic engineered to perform
avoid: athlete endorsements the brief can't back
picks.ad_angle: Recycled doesn't mean compromised — technical fabric that holds up to your fourth session of the week.

picks.name: The Sustainability Buyer
picks.why_plausible: Sustainable_apparel is their lead affinity and the brief's core claim is recycled ocean plastic, a specific rather than vague eco claim; medium price sensitivity with a $92 AOV fits the premium tier.
lean_into: specific sustainability claims (ocean plastic, material sourcing)
picks.ad_angle: Name the material and the math: what 'made from recycled ocean plastic' actually means, for a skeptic who reads supply chains.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Female-skewed, 28-40, with fitness and wellness affinities and low price_sensitivity at a $95 AOV — she already dresses for tracked workouts and pays premiums for products she can interrogate.
lean_into: outcome-focused: fit, support, how it feels in training
avoid: unproven 'science' claims the brief doesn't support
picks.ad_angle: Your gear as part of the system — material transparency and fit worth auditing, same as everything else you put on your body.

picks.name: The Affluent Classic
picks.why_plausible: Female, low price sensitivity, $145 AOV and buys apparel for longevity rather than trend — premium activewear for walking, pilates and travel is a natural extension of her classic_apparel and travel affinities.
picks.ad_angle: Pieces you'll keep for years — understated, well-made activewear that outlasts the trend cycle.

picks.name: The Gifter
picks.why_plausible: Gift mode shoppers with low price sensitivity and a $95 AOV buy premium_basics and apparel, and a recognizable-value activewear piece is a safe, impressive gift for a woman who works out.
lean_into: a gift with a story (the ocean-plastic origin makes it easy to talk about)
avoid: niche sizing/fit complexity that makes gifting risky
picks.ad_angle: The activewear gift that comes with a story worth telling when she opens it.

plan.summary: Budget leans on the two placements with a real purchase-moment link — Studiogrid class bookers who need something to work out in and Stride & Stem's sustainability-responsive women's footwear buyers — with values- and demographics-led tests at Pantrygood, Daily Form, Everbody and Marlowe, while Linden Park drops out for its 50-70, conservative-sensibility audience and the two activewear sellers stay excluded as competitors.

recommended.name: Studiogrid

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 74% female; high income for premium price

recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a loose fitness adjacency, but the purchase moment is the sharpest in the catalog: someone who just booked a yoga class or personal training session needs something to wear to it. The notes confirm active spend on fitness, not just interest in it, and the audience is 74% female at high income, which suits an $85 premium piece.
recommended.rationale: Shoppers here have just paid for a class ('Appointment-based booking. Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness'), and yoga/personal-training bookings are the exact moment women shop for activewear; 74% female, high income supports the premium price.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: The $85 offer is about 2× the $42 typical booking, so the ask is larger than the basket the shopper just committed to.

recommended.name: Stride & Stem

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 94% female; high income for premium price

recommended.tier_reason: Scored down on reach and flagged for footwear adjacency, but shoes are not a substitute for activewear apparel, and this is a demonstrated buyer of premium sustainable women's apparel: the notes say sustainability claims already convert here, and the $142 basket makes $85 an easy step down.
recommended.rationale: Notes say 'Sustainability and machine-washable claims resonate' with a 94%-female, high-income base, so the recycled-ocean-plastic story lands on shoppers who just paid $142 for sustainable women's footwear.
recommended.risk: Only 3.2M monthly impressions, so volume will be thin; the audience is framed as professional/workwear rather than workout-focused.

test.name: Marlowe & Co.

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 96% female; high income for premium price

test.rationale: Affluent women buying $112 premium workwear who 'responds to quality messaging' may add athleisure, but the 45-65 skew sits above the brand's core buyer and the notes warn of 'Lower impulse'.

evidence.quote: Lower impulse but high AOV. Responds to quality messaging

test.risk: Workwear buyers at 45-65 may not be regular workout shoppers, and low impulse hurts a post-checkout ask.

test.name: Pantrygood

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 71% female; high income for premium price

test.rationale: Notes say shoppers are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' at a $86 basket that matches the $85 offer, so the recycled-plastic claim should land; the open question is whether grocery checkout converts on apparel.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: No purchase-moment link to apparel; the connection is values only, so conversion could be much weaker than the audience suggests.

test.name: Everbody

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 99% female; mid income for premium price

test.adjacent_conflict: sells intimates, womens_apparel, a close substitute
test.rationale: 99% female apparel buyers at an $89 basket that matches the offer price; worth testing whether 'Inclusive sizing' shoppers respond to a premium activewear range whose size run is unstated.

evidence.quote: Inclusive sizing across the full range

test.risk: If the brand's sizing is limited, fit-focused plus-size shoppers will bounce; mid income also makes $85 a stretch here.

test.name: Daily Form

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 89% female; mid-high income for premium price

test.rationale: Women's supplement subscribers (89% female, 22-42) are fitness- and wellness-engaged, the closest behavioural proxy for regular workouts; the uncertainty is the $85 ask against a $38 basket.
test.risk: Offer is 2.2× the typical order, and the audience is 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims', so sustainability messaging must be concrete.

test_plan.hypothesis: Affluent women buying $112 premium workwear who 'responds to quality messaging' may add athleisure, but the 45-65 skew sits above the brand's core buyer and the notes warn of 'Lower impulse'.
test_plan.risk: Workwear buyers at 45-65 may not be regular workout shoppers, and low impulse hurts a post-checkout ask.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $25.50 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $33.15 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.hypothesis: Notes say shoppers are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' at a $86 basket that matches the $85 offer, so the recycled-plastic claim should land; the open question is whether grocery checkout converts on apparel.
test_plan.risk: No purchase-moment link to apparel; the connection is values only, so conversion could be much weaker than the audience suggests.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $25.50 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $33.15 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.hypothesis: 99% female apparel buyers at an $89 basket that matches the offer price; worth testing whether 'Inclusive sizing' shoppers respond to a premium activewear range whose size run is unstated.
test_plan.risk: If the brand's sizing is limited, fit-focused plus-size shoppers will bounce; mid income also makes $85 a stretch here.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $25.50 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $33.15 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.hypothesis: Women's supplement subscribers (89% female, 22-42) are fitness- and wellness-engaged, the closest behavioural proxy for regular workouts; the uncertainty is the $85 ask against a $38 basket.
test_plan.risk: Offer is 2.2× the typical order, and the audience is 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims', so sustainability messaging must be concrete.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $25.50 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $33.15 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a first order around $85, between Lululemon and Girlfriend Collective pricing.
Assumed a core audience of women roughly 25-44.
Assumed one-time purchases rather than a subscription.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 budget goes to two placements with a real purchase-moment link: Studiogrid class bookers who need something to work out in, and Stride & Stem's sustainability-responsive women's footwear buyers. The remaining $1,500 test budget is split evenly across Pantrygood, Everbody, Daily Form and Marlowe & Co. to learn whether values or demographics alone convert on apparel without a workout-adjacent purchase. Linden Park was dropped for its older, conservative audience, and activewear sellers are excluded as competitors.
uncertainties: The $85 first order is inferred, and the $25.50 target cost per new customer is built on it as 30% of that value.
One-time purchase is assumed, so the plan requires the first order to pay back acquisition with no repeat value counted.
The brand's size run is unstated, which is exactly what the Everbody test with inclusive-sizing shoppers depends on.
questions: What is your actual average first order value and margin on it?
Do customers repeat or subscribe, or is each order one-time?
What sizes do you carry, and can you substantiate the recycled ocean plastic claim in specifics?
